beliefs.practice: Use a single, global PyMongo MongoClient instance (singleton) reused across the app, created once at process start and closed on shutdown; do not create a new MongoClient per request or agent.

Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable at runtime (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) and never commit the secret to source control or write it to logs; provide a .env.example with a placeholder instead.
Enable TLS/SSL in the MongoClient connection options and set reasonable timeouts (serverSelectionTimeoutMS, connectTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS) to fail fast and avoid hung requests.

Configure the MongoClient connection pool and maxPoolSize appropriate to the process concurrency (e.g., web worker threads/processes) rather than leaving defaults; tune socket/heartbeat timeouts for cloud latency.

Use least-privilege credentials: create a dedicated DB user for the orchestration app with only the required roles (read/write for sample_banking_04, no admin privileges), and rotate credentials using secrets manager or Azure Key Vault where possible.
Seed scripts must be idempotent: check for existing documents/indexes before insert/create so repeated runs do not duplicate data or throw errors (use upsert or createIndex with check).

Create indexes for the exact fields and compound order used by queries (e.g., reporting_period, account_id, workflow_id, status) and test queries with explain() to ensure index usage; add projections to queries to return only needed fields.

Add a TTL index for ephemeral workflow/log documents (e.g., workflow_status documents) to automatically expire old runs rather than indefinitely retaining them, using a date field and expireAfterSeconds.

For vector search, store vectors as arrays of floats with a consistent dimensionality and similarity convention (e.g., normalized for cosine) and create an explicit vector index with tuned parameters (index type HNSW/IVF and params like m/efConstruction/efSearch) matching query-time settings.

When using vector indexes, ensure index creation is idempotent and that vector field types and lengths are validated at write time; avoid mixing vectors of different dimensionalities in the same field/collection.

Protect long-running multi-step orchestrations by recording each step's status as a document (workflow-run document) with timestamps and a resumable state so the orchestrator can resume or retry idempotently after failures.

Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient network and server errors (e.g., network timeouts, 5xx/TransientMongoErrors), and ensure retries are safe (idempotent or guarded by deduplication keys/workflow state).

Use multi-document transactions only when necessary for strong atomicity across documents/collections; keep transactions small and short-lived, and test against the live cluster because mongomock unit tests do not fully emulate transaction semantics.

Avoid storing very large documents or huge arrays in a single document; break large time-series or large lists into bucketed documents or separate collections to stay well under MongoDB document-size limits and to keep updates efficient.

Include a schema_version or document_version field on documents and write migration scripts for schema changes so orchestrated processes know how to validate/upgrade older documents during validation/filling steps.

Run explain() or use the cluster's profiler and Azure monitoring (metrics/alerts) to validate query performance and to identify slow queries; iterate index design based on actual query plans rather than guessing.

Do not store secrets, raw PII, or full unmasked regulatory documents in workflow logs; redact or encrypt sensitive fields before writing them into DocumentDB and restrict access via DB roles and network controls.

Write integration tests that run against the live DocumentDB cluster for features mongomock cannot emulate (vector indexes, explain plans, cluster-level index parameters, transactions), and mark unit tests using mongomock as limited-fidelity only.
